title: Why do Indonesian Ambrosia Beetles Carry Eggs on Their Heads?
content: Quowim, Anggik, Mia, and Jiri are sitting in front of a tiny field dormitory, 1,600 meters above sea level, at the foot of the Arjuna volcano in Java, Indonesia. Behind us is a rainforest, complete with melodious birds, fantastical bugs, and monkeys occasionally darting out to pilfer from the garbage can. We have been sawing, clipping, and chipping away at a large piece of dead wood speckled with miniature piles of sawdust. We are following a tiny tunnel deep into the garnet-colored heartwood. Clip! The last chunk of the wood flies off and reveals a creature that looks more like a skinny microscopic alien than a beetle. Baiocis—the tiniest of the ambrosia beetles, only as thin as about three human hairs, but long and bendy. How do these things fly from a tree to tree? How do they chew these half-foot-long tunnels in hard wood? What symbiotic fungi do they imbibe?
